claim: Giving up the fruit of action ranks above practice, knowledge and meditation, and peace follows that giving up at once.

heals.why: peace is placed right after releasing the grip on results, not after mastering meditation
the wanting that rides on every outcome is what is set down

cultivates.why: peace follows immediately on giving up the fruit
names letting go of results as the step open even to one who cannot meditate

needs: the reader is acting and anxious about outcomes; the verse closes the ladder of options in 12.8-11

commentary.reading: Shankara reads the ranking as praise of renouncing the fruit, meant for one who cannot manage the higher means of 12.8-11; Ramanuja reads each step as the easier means leading to the next.

claim: The devotee dear to God hates no being, is friendly, compassionate, free of mine and ego, even-minded and forgiving.

heals.why: pictures a life with no hatred toward any being, a direction for one tired of carrying ill will

cultivates.why: friendliness to all beings is the first mark named
compassion is named as a mark of the one dear to God
forgiveness closes the list

needs: a reader who already wants to grow in devotion; it is a portrait, not a remedy for a fresh hurt

commentary.reading: Shankara: these are the qualities of the renunciate established in knowledge, and they serve as practice for the seeker; the sentence completes in 12.14 with 'he is dear to me'.

line_issue: The verse describes a person dear to God; the line turns it into a string of commands and drops the devotional frame. Corrected: 'One who hates no being, who is friendly and kind, free of mine and ego, steady in pain and joy, and forgiving: such a devotee is dear to me.'

claim: One who neither disturbs the world nor is disturbed by it, free of elation, intolerance, fear and agitation, is dear to God.

heals.why: holds up a mind that the world cannot agitate, as a place to stand

cultivates.why: neither troubling others nor being troubled is the peace described
freedom from fear and agitation is named as a mark

commentary.reading: Shankara glosses amarsha as intolerance and udvega as agitation; one free of these four is dear to the Lord. Ramanuja takes them as feelings directed at other beings.

line_issue: A description is turned into a command and 'is dear to me' is dropped. Corrected: 'One who unsettles no one and is unsettled by no one, free of elation, resentment, fear and agitation, is dear to me.'

claim: The devotee is the same to enemy and friend, in honour and dishonour, heat and cold, pleasure and pain, unattached.

cultivates.why: the same toward friend and foe, honour and insult
free of attachment is the closing mark

needs: not as a reply to a fresh insult or injury

commentary.reading: Part of the marks of the devotee dear to God (12.13-20); the sentence completes in 12.19. Shankara applies it to the renunciate established in knowledge.

claim: One to whom blame and praise are equal, silent, content with anything, homeless, steady-minded and devoted, is dear to God.

heals.why: content with whatever comes, so praise is no longer a need

cultivates.why: contentment with whatever comes is named directly
blame and praise weigh the same

commentary.reading: Shankara: content with whatever maintains the body, without a fixed dwelling, of steady understanding about the highest truth; such a devotee is dear to the Lord.

line_issue: 'Rooted in steadiness, not status' is invented; aniketa means without a fixed home, and the devotion and 'dear to me' are dropped. Corrected: 'Praise and blame weigh the same to them. Quiet, content with whatever comes, at home anywhere, steady in mind and full of devotion: that person is dear to me.'

claim: Desire, anger and greed are the threefold gate of hell that ruins the self; one should give up all three.

cultivates.why: names the three impulses to watch before they ruin a person

commentary.reading: Shankara: these three are the door to hell and destroy the self, meaning they leave a person unfit for any human goal; giving them up is the root of all good.

claim: Speech that causes no distress, that is true, pleasant and beneficial, along with regular sacred study, is austerity of speech.

heals.why: gives a four part test to run before speaking in heat: no wound, true, kind, useful

cultivates.why: words chosen to be true, kind and helpful build goodwill

commentary.reading: Shankara: all four qualities must be present together; speech lacking any one of them is not austerity of speech.

claim: Each person's faith follows their inner nature; a person is made of faith, and is what their faith is.

cultivates.why: asks one to look at what one actually trusts, since that shows what one is
treats faith as the stuff a person is made of

commentary.reading: Shankara: sattva here is the inner organ shaped by past impressions; faith follows it, and a person is known by the faith they hold. It introduces the three kinds of faith by guna.

line_issue: The line reads like 'belief makes reality'. The verse says faith follows one's inner nature and shows what one is. Corrected: 'Everyone's faith follows their inner nature. A person is made of their faith: what you trust in shows who you are.'

claim: The doer free of attachment and self-talk, full of steadiness and zeal, unmoved by success or failure, is called sattvic.

depicts.why: pictures the worker who is full of steadiness and zest and is not shaken either way

cultivates.why: steadiness is named as what the best doer carries
zeal is named beside steadiness
unchanged by success or failure

commentary.reading: Shankara: anahamvadi is one who does not speak of himself as the doer; dhriti is firmness and utsaha is effort; such a doer is sattvic.

claim: Sattvic happiness is like poison at first and nectar in the end, born of the clarity of one's understanding of the self.

heals.why: the early bitterness of discipline is the mark of the lasting kind of happiness, not a reason to stop

cultivates.why: gives a reason to stay through the hard beginning
names clarity of mind as the source of this happiness

commentary.reading: Shankara: it is like poison at first because of the labour of knowledge, dispassion, meditation and absorption; it is born of the clarity of the intellect concerning the self.

line_issue: 'That joy is worth it' adds a verdict and drops the source the verse names. Corrected: 'Some happiness tastes like poison at first and like nectar in the end. It comes from a mind made clear about itself.'

claim: Rajasic happiness comes from the senses meeting their objects, like nectar at first and poison in the end.

heals.why: shows the arc of sense pleasure, sweet first and bitter after, so the pull can be seen through

cultivates.why: a test for telling two kinds of happiness apart by how they end

commentary.reading: Shankara: it is like poison in the end because it wears away strength, vigour, wisdom and wealth and leads to wrongdoing.

claim: One's own duty done imperfectly is better than another's done well; work set by one's nature brings no fault.

heals.why: one's own imperfect path outranks a perfect copy of someone else's
settles the doubt of whether to trade one's own work for a more admired one

cultivates.why: self-respect in doing one's own work, flaws included

commentary.reading: Shankara and Ramanuja read svadharma as the duty laid down by one's station and inborn nature; the app's 'honest fit with your own nature' is a modern extension of the svabhava clause, not the commentators' reading.
commentary.source: Shankara and Ramanuja on 18.47; same teaching as 3.35

claim: Krishna has taught the most secret knowledge; Arjuna should reflect on it fully and then do as he wishes.

heals.why: the teacher hands the decision back: think it through fully, then choose
the choice stays with the one who must act

cultivates.why: full reflection before acting is the instruction
the choice made after reflection is one's own

needs: the teaching before it; a closing verse, best in the last days of a plan

commentary.reading: Shankara: having taught the whole scripture, the Lord asks Arjuna to reflect on all of it and then act as he sees fit. Krishna goes on in 18.64-66 to give his most secret word.

line_issue: 'I've told you all I know' is not what the verse says; it calls this knowledge the most secret of secrets. Corrected: 'I have given you this teaching, the most hidden of all. Think it through fully, then do as you choose.'

claim: Giving up all dharmas and taking refuge in Krishna alone, one is freed by him from all sins; do not grieve.

heals.why: the Lord takes on the freeing from every wrong, so the verdict is no longer carried alone
refuge in one who promises to free you
the teaching ends with 'do not grieve' backed by a promise

cultivates.why: taking refuge in him alone is the instruction
the promise removes the fear of what one's wrongs will cost

needs: a devotional reader and the teaching before it; a resolution verse for the last days of a plan, never Day 1 to 3

commentary.reading: Shankara: giving up all action, righteous and unrighteous, take refuge in the one Self of all; this is knowledge with renunciation. Ramanuja: give up the sense of doership and fruit in all duties and hold the Lord alone as the means; in a second reading, give up the expiations for past sins that block devotion.

line_issue: The line drops 'abandoning all dharmas' and flattens 'do not grieve' into 'don't worry'. Corrected: 'Set down every other support and take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all your wrongs. Do not grieve.'

claim: Arjuna grieves for those not to be grieved for while talking wisdom; the wise grieve for neither the dead nor the living.

heals.why: names the confusion of grieving while arguing wisely, and opens the teaching on what does not die

needs: the scene: Arjuna has just asked to be taught (2.7); only as the opening of the 2.11-30 teaching, never alone

commentary.reading: Shankara: this verse is the seed of the whole teaching; grief and delusion are the root of samsara and only knowledge of the self removes them. The 'wise' are those who know the self. Madhusudana notes the gentle irony in 'words of wisdom'.

line_issue: 'Talking like you know better' turns a teacher's opening into a jab and drops the second half. Corrected: 'You grieve for those who need no grieving, though your words sound wise. The wise do not grieve for the living or for the dead.'

claim: As the self passes through childhood, youth and age in this body, so it takes another body; the steady are not bewildered.

heals.why: the one you knew stayed the same through every change of body, and stays through the last one
death is placed in line with changes already lived through
the steady person is not confused by the change

cultivates.why: points to the one who remains while the body's stages pass
the steady one is not thrown

needs: openness to a self that outlasts the body; not the first word to a fresh loss

commentary.reading: Shankara: as the self stays unchanged through childhood, youth and age, so it stays unchanged in taking another body; the wise are not deluded about this.

line_issue: 'The next change' hides that the verse speaks of death and another body, which lets it be served for midlife or an empty nest. Corrected: 'Childhood, youth and old age pass through this one body, and the self remains. In the same way it passes on to another body. The steady are not shaken by this.'

claim: Sense contacts bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain; they come and go and do not last, so bear them.

heals.why: what is felt now is named as a passing contact, not a permanent state
pain is placed among things that come and go

cultivates.why: bearing what passes without being moved
titiksha, forbearance toward passing discomfort

needs: the pain is a passing discomfort, not an ongoing harm someone is doing

commentary.reading: Shankara: cold and heat, pleasure and pain are impermanent because they come and go; therefore endure them, without elation or dejection.

claim: The self is never born and never dies; unborn, eternal and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.

heals.why: what you loved in the person was never born and does not end with the body
what you are is not ended by the death of the body

cultivates.why: states the nature of the self directly: unborn, lasting, ancient
nothing that can happen to the body reaches it

needs: openness to a self distinct from the body; not the first word to a fresh loss

commentary.reading: Shankara: the verse denies of the self all six changes that things undergo: birth, existence, growth, change, decline and death.

claim: As a person discards worn-out clothes for new ones, the embodied self discards worn-out bodies and enters new ones.

heals.why: the one who wore the body is not gone with it
dying is pictured as a change of clothes

cultivates.why: the wearer is other than what is worn

needs: belief in rebirth; fits the passing of the old, not an untimely death

commentary.reading: Shankara: as one puts aside worn garments and takes others, the self, itself unchanged, leaves worn bodies and enters new ones.

claim: Death is certain for the born and birth for the dead; so one should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.

heals.why: offers acceptance: what happened is what happens to everyone who is born
death is named as certain, so it need not be fought in the mind

cultivates.why: steadiness before what cannot be changed

needs: some distance from the loss; argues from the common view of birth and death

commentary.reading: Shankara: from 2.26 Krishna grants, for argument, the common view that the self is born and dies; even then grief is not fitting, because death and rebirth are unavoidable.

claim: Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike, one should fight; so no sin is incurred.

heals.why: both outcomes are set level before stepping in
ends the wavering with a way to act that carries no wrong

cultivates.why: gain and loss, win and defeat held alike

needs: the action in question is one's rightful duty; said to a warrior before a just war

commentary.reading: Shankara: an incidental instruction; fighting as one's own duty with evenness toward pleasure and pain, gain and loss, brings no sin.

claim: On this path no beginning is lost and no harm results; even a little of this dharma protects from great fear.

heals.why: a small sincere effort already protects
answers the worry that an unfinished effort is a wasted one

cultivates.why: frees a person to begin, since nothing begun here is lost
trust that sincere effort counts
supports the decision to start small

commentary.reading: Shankara: unlike farming, a beginning in karma yoga is never wasted, and unlike medicine it has no contrary result; the great fear is the fear of samsara, of birth and death.

claim: One has a right to action alone, never to its fruits; fruit must not be the motive, nor inaction the refuge.

heals.why: the result was never in your hands; the work is
the fruit is taken away as the reason for acting

cultivates.why: work done without the fruit as motive stays even
lets go of the claim on results while keeping the work

commentary.reading: Shankara: your entitlement is to action only, not to its results; do not through craving become the cause of the fruit, and do not turn to inaction either.

claim: Established in yoga, one should act without attachment, the same in success and failure; this evenness is called yoga.

heals.why: success and failure are held as one before the work begins

cultivates.why: evenness is given as the very definition of yoga

commentary.reading: Shankara: act for the Lord's sake, giving up even the wish that he be pleased; evenness in success and failure is yoga.

claim: One joined to wisdom sheds both merit and demerit here; so strive for yoga, which is skill in action.

heals.why: work done with an even mind does not bind the one who does it

cultivates.why: the skill meant is evenness of mind in work
understanding, not effort alone, is what frees

commentary.reading: Shankara: the skill is that actions, which by nature bind, do not bind when done with evenness of mind offered to the Lord; it is not skill in the sense of doing work efficiently.

line_issue: 'Doing the work well' leads with the popular misreading and the first half is dropped. Corrected: 'With this understanding, a person is no longer bound by the good or bad results of what they do. That is the skill in action called yoga.'

claim: One whose mind is unshaken in sorrow, without craving in pleasure, free of attachment, fear and anger, is a steady-minded sage.

heals.why: the steady mind is pictured as free of anger
free of fear is one of its marks
a mind that sorrow does not agitate is shown as possible

cultivates.why: unshaken in sorrow
no craving when things go well, no agitation when they do not

needs: a wish for steadiness; not a reply to fresh grief or injury

commentary.reading: Shankara: in the scriptures on the self the marks of the realised are taught as the practices of the seeker; so this portrait is also a discipline.

claim: When one withdraws the senses from their objects as a tortoise draws in its limbs, one's wisdom is firmly established.

heals.why: a way to pull attention back from what scatters it
the senses are drawn in before the pull grows

cultivates.why: wisdom stays set when the senses are gathered

commentary.reading: Shankara: the one devoted to knowledge draws the senses in from all objects, as a tortoise draws in its limbs from fear.

claim: Dwelling on sense objects breeds attachment to them; attachment breeds desire; desire breeds anger.

heals.why: the chain starts with what the mind keeps dwelling on, so it can be caught there
attachment is shown as something that grows from repeated dwelling

cultivates.why: lets a person trace anger back to its first step

needs: the trouble really is craving, fixation or anger from thwarted wanting; not a general diagnosis for grief, fear or being wronged

commentary.reading: Shankara: thinking of objects produces liking for them; from liking comes thirst; when that is obstructed by something, anger arises.

claim: Anger breeds delusion, delusion loss of memory, that the ruin of understanding, and with understanding ruined one perishes.

heals.why: shows what anger costs step by step: clear sight, the memory of what one knows, then judgement

cultivates.why: knowing the sequence gives a reason to stop at the first step

needs: the anger is one's own reactivity; never told to someone whose anger answers a real wrong

commentary.reading: Shankara: delusion is the loss of discrimination between right and wrong; memory is of what scripture and teacher have taught; ruin of the intellect is unfitness for any human goal.

claim: Without discipline there is no understanding or contemplation; without contemplation no peace; without peace, no happiness.

heals.why: explains why a scattered mind cannot find rest: peace needs a gathered mind first

cultivates.why: peace is placed as the ground of happiness

commentary.reading: Shankara: the ayukta is one whose mind is not collected; bhavana is steady application to knowledge of the self; without it there is no peace, and without peace no happiness.

claim: Overcome by faint-heartedness and confused about dharma, Arjuna asks Krishna, as a surrendered student, to say what is surely best.

depicts.why: a capable man says he can no longer tell what is right
'my mind is confused about dharma', said in the first person
he asks to be taught as a student

cultivates.why: turning to someone wiser and saying 'teach me' is itself the first step

commentary.reading: Shankara: karpanya is the poverty of one who does not know the self; with this verse Arjuna becomes a disciple and the teaching can begin. Plain sense: his nature is overcome by weakness and he surrenders as a student.

line_issue: The line drops the confession of being overcome and flattens surrender into 'ready to learn'. Corrected: 'Something in me has given way, and I can no longer tell what is right. Tell me for certain what is best. I am your student and I have come to you. Teach me.'

claim: As the full, unmoving ocean receives the waters, one whom desires enter thus attains peace, not one who craves desires.

heals.why: wanting can arrive without moving the one it arrives in
peace belongs to the one desires do not stir, not the one who chases them

cultivates.why: the ocean stays full and still while rivers enter
fullness that does not depend on what flows in

commentary.reading: Shankara: as waters enter the ocean without changing it, desires enter the sage without disturbing him; he attains peace, not the one who longs for objects.

line_issue: The line turns the image into an instruction and drops the conclusion. Corrected: 'Rivers pour into the ocean and it stays full and unmoved. The one whom desires enter in that way finds peace, not the one who chases them.'

claim: Whatever a great person does, others do; whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

cultivates.why: one's conduct is itself what others receive and follow

commentary.reading: Shankara: whatever the foremost person does and whatever he accepts as authority, ordinary people follow; hence even the wise should act for the holding together of the world.

claim: One's own duty done imperfectly is better than another's done well; death in one's own duty is better, another's is fearful.

heals.why: one's own imperfect path outranks a perfect copy of someone else's
settles the doubt of whether to trade one's own work for a more admired one

cultivates.why: self-respect in doing one's own work, flaws included

commentary.reading: Shankara: under the pull of like and dislike one mistakes another's duty for one's own; one's own, even without merit, is better. Ramanuja: one's own dharma here is karma yoga, natural and safe, against a path one is not fit for.
commentary.source: Shankara and Ramanuja on 3.35; same teaching as 18.47

claim: Desire, which becomes anger, born of rajas, all-devouring and greatly sinful, is the enemy here.

heals.why: the force is named and made an opponent one can know
anger is shown as desire in another form
what drove the act is named as an enemy to be known, not as who you are

cultivates.why: knowing the enemy is the first instruction

needs: answers Arjuna's question in 3.36: what drives a person to do wrong even against their will

commentary.reading: Shankara: it is desire itself which, when obstructed, turns into anger; born of rajas, never satisfied, it is the enemy of the whole world.

claim: One should do one's allotted work, for action is better than inaction; even bodily life is impossible without action.

heals.why: doing the work that is yours is better than waiting, and even living needs action

cultivates.why: settles the question of whether to act at all

needs: answers the wish to withdraw from work; not for someone who is exhausted or burnt out

commentary.reading: Shankara: niyata karma is the obligatory duty one is qualified for; action is better than inaction, since without it even the body's upkeep is not possible.

claim: In whatever way people approach Krishna, in that way he receives them; people everywhere follow his path.

heals.why: one's own way of turning to God is met as it is
no approach is too small to be received

cultivates.why: trust that the turning is answered in kind
invites approach in whatever form one can manage

needs: a reader open to God

commentary.reading: Shankara: the Lord rewards each in the way they seek him, giving fruits to those who want fruits and liberation to those who seek it. Sridhara: even those who worship other gods follow his path. The line's 'every path leads to me' follows the Sridhara reading.

claim: Content with what comes unasked, beyond the opposites, free of envy, even in success and failure, one acts and is not bound.

heals.why: free of envy is named beside contentment with what comes
content with what arrives unasked

cultivates.why: contentment with whatever comes on its own
the same in success and failure

commentary.reading: Shankara: describes the knower who lives on what comes unsought, is untouched by the pairs of opposites and bears no ill will; though acting, he is not bound.

claim: That knowledge is learned by prostration, questioning and service; the wise who have seen the truth will teach it.

cultivates.why: real questioning of one who knows is named as the way to learn
humility before a teacher who has seen the truth

needs: a reader who is actively seeking a teacher or deeper study; it is filler when served for anxiety, doubt or self-worth

commentary.reading: Shankara: go to the teachers, bow fully, ask how bondage and liberation come about, and serve; only knowledge taught by those who have realised the truth bears fruit.

claim: One with faith, intent on it and with senses restrained gains knowledge, and with knowledge soon reaches supreme peace.

heals.why: faith and steady application are named as what carries one through to understanding

cultivates.why: faith is the first condition of gaining knowledge
supreme peace follows knowledge soon

commentary.reading: Shankara: faith, devotion to the means and control of the senses together bring knowledge without fail, and knowledge quickly brings the supreme peace of liberation.

claim: Whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, the Lord brings himself forth.

heals.why: when wrong gains ground it is not left unanswered
the one who was wronged is told that the rise of wrong draws God's own response

cultivates.why: trust that right is upheld

needs: a reader open to God

commentary.reading: Shankara: when the dharma of the stations of life declines and adharma rises, the Lord manifests himself through his own maya.

claim: One who acts offering actions to Brahman without attachment is untouched by sin, as a lotus leaf by water.

heals.why: the claim on one's work is given away, so the work stops clinging

cultivates.why: acting with attachment set down
the work is placed in God's hands

needs: a reader open to offering work to God

commentary.reading: Shankara: placing all actions in the Lord, acting as a servant acts for a master, without attachment even to the fruit; such a one is not stained.

line_issue: The verse is about offering one's actions to God and not being stained by wrong; the line turns it into not letting workplace mess soak in. Corrected: 'Offer your work to God and let go of your claim on it. Then wrong does not cling to you, as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.'

claim: Pleasures born of contact are sources of sorrow, with a beginning and an end; the wise do not delight in them.

heals.why: contact pleasures are shown to carry their own ending and sorrow
a reason to stop staking joy on what begins and ends

cultivates.why: the wise look at where a pleasure ends
not delighting in what is bound to pass

commentary.reading: Shankara: enjoyments born of the contact of senses and objects are sources of sorrow here and hereafter and have a beginning and an end; the one who sees the truth finds no delight in them.

claim: One who can withstand the surge born of desire and anger, here before the body falls, is a yogi and is happy.

heals.why: anger is treated as a surge that can be outlasted
the pull of desire is something to withstand, not obey

cultivates.why: the capacity to hold steady while the surge passes

needs: the surge is one's own impulse, not a rightful response to harm

commentary.reading: Shankara: 'before release from the body' means as long as one lives, for the causes of these surges are endless; the one who withstands them is a yogi and happy here.

claim: Yoga is not for one who eats too much or nothing, nor for one who oversleeps or stays awake.

heals.why: names the extremes of food and sleep as what blocks steadiness

commentary.reading: Shankara: yoga does not come to one who eats beyond his measure or not at all, nor to one who sleeps or wakes too much.

claim: For one moderate in food, recreation, effort at work, sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.

heals.why: measure in food, rest, work and sleep is given as the ground of relief

cultivates.why: a measured day makes the mind light enough for practice

commentary.reading: Shankara: for one whose food, movement, effort in actions, sleep and waking are measured, yoga destroys all the sorrow of samsara.

claim: A lamp in a windless place that does not flicker is the simile for the yogi's controlled mind in meditation.

heals.why: an image of what a settled mind is like, to hold in view

cultivates.why: the unflickering flame as a picture of stillness

commentary.reading: Shankara: the simile, used by those who know yoga, is for the mind of the yogi absorbed in the self.

claim: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, one should restrain it and bring it back under the self's control.

heals.why: wandering is expected; the practice is only the returning
each time the mind runs to a worry it can be brought back

cultivates.why: patient repetition of the same return

commentary.reading: Shankara: from whatever cause the mind goes out, such as sound and the other objects, see that cause as unreal, restrain the mind from it and bring it under the sway of the self.

claim: One who sees pleasure and pain everywhere as the same by likeness to oneself is deemed the highest yogi.

heals.why: the other's pain is felt as one's own would be
before reacting, measure the other by oneself

cultivates.why: others' pain is known by one's own
others' happiness is wished as one's own

commentary.reading: Shankara: as pleasure is welcome and pain unwelcome to me, so it is to all beings; seeing this, he harms no one. Such a one, harmless and established in right vision, is the highest yogi.

claim: The mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn; restraining it seems as hard as restraining the wind.

depicts.why: Arjuna says it in his own voice: the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn
he doubts it can be held at all

commentary.reading: Shankara: the mind churns the body and senses, is strong and tough like a cord; Arjuna judges its control as hard as controlling the wind. Krishna agrees in 6.35.

claim: The mind is indeed restless and hard to restrain, but it is held by practice and dispassion.

heals.why: the teacher agrees the mind is hard to hold, then names two things that hold it
answers 'can it be done at all' with yes, by repetition and letting go

cultivates.why: practice means returning again and again
loosening the pull of what the mind runs to

commentary.reading: Shankara: practice is the repetition of the same thought on one object; dispassion is freedom from thirst for seen and unseen enjoyments, gained by seeing their defects. By these the mind is restrained.

claim: For the striver in yoga there is no ruin here or hereafter; no doer of good comes to a bad end.

heals.why: the fear that a sincere effort which falls short is wasted is answered with a promise
falling short on a good path is not ruin

cultivates.why: trust that sincere effort is kept
frees a person to try again

needs: Arjuna's question in 6.37-39 about the seeker who tries with faith and falls short; it is not a promise that good people never suffer

commentary.reading: Shankara: for the one fallen from yoga there is no loss here or in the next world; no one who does good comes to a bad state. Krishna addresses Arjuna tenderly as 'tata'.

line_issue: Out of its scene the line reads as a blanket promise that good people are never ruined, which is why it gets used as filler. The verse answers the fear of a seeker who falls short. Corrected: 'No one who sincerely tries to do good is ever lost, my friend. Not here, and not after.'

claim: One should lift oneself by oneself and not let oneself sink; the self alone is one's friend and one's enemy.

heals.why: 'do not let yourself sink' speaks straight to the pull downward
asks a person to be their own friend, not their own prosecutor
the power to rise is placed inside the person

cultivates.why: self-respect: you are the one who can lift you
a call to rise
the decision to be on one's own side

needs: some strength to act; a person in acute collapse needs to be met first

commentary.reading: Shankara: lift the self sunk in the ocean of samsara by the self; no one else is the friend who frees you, and no other enemy harms you as your own uncontrolled self does.

line_issue: 'You can be your own friend' leaves out the other half. Corrected: 'Lift yourself by your own strength and do not let yourself sink. You are your own friend, and you can be your own enemy.'

claim: For one who has conquered oneself the self is a friend; for one who has not, the self acts as an enemy.

heals.why: explains why the mind seems to work against you: it has not yet been brought under your own hand

cultivates.why: which side the mind is on depends on whether it is mastered
self-mastery turns the mind into an ally

commentary.reading: Shankara: the self is a friend to one who has subdued the body, senses and mind; for one who has not, his own self acts against him like an outside enemy.

claim: For the self-conquered, peaceful one, the supreme Self stays present through heat and cold, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour.

cultivates.why: the higher Self is present to the calm, self-mastered person
the same in honour and dishonour
the deep calm of one who has mastered himself

needs: not as a reply to a fresh insult or injury

commentary.reading: Shankara: for the one who has mastered himself and is serene, the supreme Self becomes directly his own self, and he is even in cold and heat, honour and dishonour.

line_issue: 'You stay centred' drops what the verse says is present. Corrected: 'For one who is self-mastered and calm, the higher Self is steadily present, in heat and cold, pleasure and pain, honour and insult.'

claim: For those who worship Krishna with undivided thought, ever devoted, he himself carries what they lack and guards what they have.

heals.why: the worry of getting and keeping is carried by God for the one wholly turned to him
what you have is guarded

cultivates.why: undivided turning to him is the condition
trust that he provides
provision and protection are promised

needs: a devotional reader; the promise is to those wholly given to him, not a guarantee of money

commentary.reading: Shankara: yoga is gaining what one lacks and kshema is keeping what one has; for those who see nothing apart from him and do not strive for themselves, the Lord himself carries both.

claim: Whoever offers a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with devotion, Krishna accepts that loving offering of the pure-hearted.

heals.why: the smallest thing given with love is accepted; you do not need to bring much

cultivates.why: offering even a little as thanks
devotion is what makes the gift, not its size

needs: a reader open to God

commentary.reading: Shankara: devotion is easy; the Lord accepts even a leaf or water when it is brought with love by one of pure mind. Sridhara stresses how easily he is pleased.

claim: Seeing his own kin arrayed and eager for battle, Arjuna is overcome by deep pity and speaks in despair.

depicts.why: he speaks while sinking, at the sight of his own people on the other side
the people he must oppose are his own

commentary.reading: Shankara treats Arjuna's pity as born of attachment and delusion, the grief the teaching will remove; Sanjaya's words frame it: overcome by deep compassion, despairing, he spoke.

line_issue: The line is a narrator's comment, not the verse. Corrected: 'When I see my own people standing here ready to fight, Krishna, pity and sorrow come over me.'

claim: Arjuna's limbs fail, his mouth dries, his body trembles, the bow slips, he cannot stand and his mind reels.

depicts.why: the body gives way first: limbs, mouth, skin, grip
trembling and hair standing on end
'my mind is whirling', said from inside it

commentary.reading: The plain sense is not disputed: Arjuna reports the bodily signs of his grief and fear. The record's Sanskrit runs 1.29-30 while its translation covers only 1.29.

line_issue: 'A panic attack, not a hero' is a modern diagnosis and a contrast line; the verse is Arjuna speaking. Corrected: 'My limbs give way and my mouth goes dry. My body shakes, the bow slips from my hand, and my mind is spinning.'

claim: Having spoken, Arjuna sat down in the chariot, dropping bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

depicts.why: he puts down what he does best and sits
his mind is overwhelmed by grief

commentary.reading: Plain narrative sense: Arjuna, his mind shaken by grief, lets go of bow and arrows and sits down in the chariot. This is the collapse that the teaching answers.

claim: Out of compassion, dwelling in their hearts, Krishna destroys the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.

heals.why: the darkness of not knowing is cleared from within, by grace
he is said to live in the heart of the one who loves him

cultivates.why: understanding is promised to those who stay turned to him
the clearing is his doing, out of compassion

needs: a devotional reader; 'them' are the devotees of 10.9-10

commentary.reading: Shankara: dwelling in the inner organ, the Lord destroys the darkness of false notions with the lamp of discriminating knowledge, fed by the oil of devotion and fanned by the wind of meditation.

claim: Whatever being is glorious, prosperous or powerful arises from a fraction of Krishna's splendour.

heals.why: another's excellence is a spark of God, not a verdict on you
one's own success is a spark of his splendour, not one's own fire

cultivates.why: excellence anywhere becomes a reason for reverence
seeing the divine in whatever shines

needs: a reader open to God

commentary.reading: Shankara: whatever has greatness, beauty or vigour, know it as born of a part of the Lord's own splendour.

claim: Arjuna should rise and win glory; his enemies are already slain by Krishna, and he is to be only the instrument.

heals.why: the outcome is not his to carry; his part is to rise and act

cultivates.why: acting as an instrument of a will larger than one's own
'therefore stand up'

needs: the scene: Krishna as Time has shown the war's end; outside it the line reads as fatalism

commentary.reading: Shankara: these warriors have already been slain by the Lord as Time; Arjuna is only the occasion, and should rise and win fame.

line_issue: The line removes that the warriors are 'already slain by me' and reads as a general 'it is fated'. If used, keep the speaker. Corrected: 'So rise and do your part. What must happen here I have already done; be my instrument.'

claim: Arjuna asks forgiveness for addressing Krishna casually as a friend and slighting him in jest, not knowing his greatness.

depicts.why: he sees he took someone great for granted and says so plainly

cultivates.why: asking forgiveness without excuses

needs: the scene of the cosmic form helps; the feeling of having taken someone for granted carries on its own

commentary.reading: Plain sense, shared by the commentators: seeing the cosmic form, Arjuna begs pardon for what he said out of carelessness or affection, treating the Lord as a companion.

claim: Prostrating, Arjuna begs the Lord to bear with him as father with son, friend with friend, lover with beloved.

depicts.why: he bows fully and asks to be borne with

cultivates.why: bowing down and asking for grace
shows how forgiveness is asked for: with the body bowed and no excuse

needs: the reader is the one who needs to apologise, not the one who was hurt

commentary.reading: Shankara: as a father forgives a son's fault, a friend a friend's, a lover the beloved's, so the Lord should forgive him.

claim: One who works for Krishna, holds him supreme, is devoted, unattached and without enmity toward any being, comes to him.

heals.why: no enmity toward any being is one of the five marks

cultivates.why: holding him as the highest goal
work done for him
without enmity toward any being

needs: a devotional reader

commentary.reading: Shankara calls this verse the essence of the whole Gita teaching, gathered up for practice. Without enmity even toward those who do one great harm.

line_issue: The line is a list of commands and drops the promise. Corrected: 'One who works for me, holds me highest, loves me, lets go of clinging and bears no enmity toward any being comes to me.'

claim: If unable even to practise, one should be intent on work for Krishna; acting for his sake too brings perfection.

heals.why: if the higher practice is beyond you, there is a step below it that still counts
failing at practice is expected and provided for

cultivates.why: work done for his sake
dedicating ordinary work to him

needs: a devotional reader who feels unable to keep a practice

commentary.reading: Shankara: if you cannot manage the yoga of practice, be devoted to doing actions for the Lord; through purity of mind, yoga and knowledge, even that leads to perfection.

claim: If unable even for that, one should take refuge in Krishna, be self-restrained, and give up the fruit of all actions.

heals.why: even the person who can do none of the higher things is given a way
the results are what is handed over

cultivates.why: giving up the fruit of all actions
done while taking refuge in him

needs: follows 12.8-10

commentary.reading: Shankara: if you cannot even work for the Lord's sake, then, relying on offering all actions to him, with mind controlled, renounce the fruit of all actions.

line_issue: The line drops 'taking refuge in me'. Corrected: 'And if even that is beyond you, then lean on me, steady yourself, and let go of the results of everything you do.'

claim: The devotee who is ever content, self-controlled, firm in resolve, with mind and intellect given to Krishna, is dear to him.

cultivates.why: always content
firm in resolve
mind and understanding given to him

needs: a devotional reader

commentary.reading: Shankara: ever content whether or not the body's needs are met, of firm conviction about the truth of the self, with mind and intellect offered to the Lord.

claim: The devotee who expects nothing, is pure, capable, impartial, untroubled and has given up all undertakings, is dear to Krishna.

heals.why: expecting nothing, so nothing is owed
'gone beyond distress' is one of the marks

cultivates.why: depending on nothing outside
untroubled and impartial

needs: not for someone who is starting or building something; the tradition reads it of one who has given up ventures

commentary.reading: Shankara: without dependence on body, senses or objects; one who has given up every undertaking prompted by desire for results here or hereafter.

line_issue: 'Not chasing every new venture' softens the verse, which says he has given up all self-seeking undertakings. Corrected: 'Expecting nothing, clean within and without, capable, impartial, untroubled, having given up every self-seeking undertaking: such a devotee is dear to me.'

claim: One who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor craves, has renounced good and bad, and is devoted, is dear to Krishna.

cultivates.why: no swing between elation and aversion
good and bad results alike are let go

needs: a settled reader; to someone grieving or hurt, 'does not grieve, does not hate' reads as a rebuke

commentary.reading: Shankara: he does not exult on getting the desired, nor hate the undesired, nor grieve at loss, nor long for what he lacks; he has given up good and bad actions.

claim: If one cannot fix the mind steadily on Krishna, one should seek to reach him through the yoga of practice.

heals.why: a mind that will not stay is expected; repeated practice is the answer
inability is met with an easier step, not blame

cultivates.why: returning the mind again and again

needs: a devotional reader

commentary.reading: Shankara: practice is withdrawing the mind from everything and fixing it again and again on the one object; by that yoga seek to reach the Lord.

line_issue: The line removes the object of the practice. Corrected: 'If you cannot yet keep your mind steadily on me, then seek to reach me through regular practice.'

claim: One who sees the supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings, the imperishable within the perishing, truly sees.

heals.why: within what perishes there is one who does not
the undying is present in everything that dies

cultivates.why: seeing the one imperishable presence in all beings
the same Lord in all

needs: openness to a self or Lord that does not die with the body

commentary.reading: Shankara: the supreme Lord is the same in all beings from Brahma to the unmoving, and does not perish when they perish; the one who sees this alone sees, all others see wrongly.

claim: Seeing the Lord equally present everywhere, one does not harm the self by the self and so reaches the highest goal.

heals.why: the one who sees the same presence in himself as everywhere stops wounding himself
the same Lord is in the one you resent

cultivates.why: the same Lord seen everywhere, including in oneself
equal vision

commentary.reading: Shankara: the ignorant 'kill the self' by taking the body for the self and not knowing their own nature; the one who sees the Lord everywhere does not, and reaches the highest.

claim: Humility, no pretence, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadiness and self-control are counted as knowledge.

heals.why: the list opens with not seeking honour and not pretending

cultivates.why: forbearance is named among the means to knowledge

needs: a seeker asking what a life aimed at knowledge looks like; a bare list otherwise

commentary.reading: Shankara: these twenty qualities (13.7-11) are called knowledge because they are the means to it; kshanti is remaining unchanged when wronged by others.

claim: Dispassion toward sense objects, absence of ego, and seeing the pain and defect in birth, death, age and sickness are knowledge.

heals.why: dispassion toward what the senses chase
absence of the 'I' that claims

cultivates.why: repeatedly seeing the pain built into birth, ageing, illness and death loosens the grip of pleasure
looking at embodied life without flattery

needs: a seeker's contemplation; cruel if shown to someone nursing a sick or ageing parent

commentary.reading: Shankara: reflecting on the defect of pain in each of birth, death, old age and disease produces dispassion toward body and sense pleasures and turns the mind to the inner self.

claim: Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness and craving arise when rajas predominates.

heals.why: the unrest is named as a rise of rajas, a passing quality of nature, and not as the person
constant starting and doing is shown as a symptom, not a virtue

cultivates.why: learning to read one's own state by its signs

commentary.reading: Shankara: ashama is the absence of calm, a ceaseless stirring of joy and craving; spriha is thirst for everything in general. These signs show that rajas has risen.

claim: The one beyond the gunas does not hate illumination, activity or delusion when present, nor long for them when gone.

heals.why: restlessness can be present without being fought
even dullness and confusion, when they come, are not hated

cultivates.why: neither hating a state while it is here nor longing for it when it leaves
inner states are watched as movements of nature

needs: answers Arjuna's question in 14.21 about the marks of one beyond the three gunas

commentary.reading: Shankara: the knower does not think 'a tamasic notion has arisen in me, I am deluded' and hate it, nor long for clarity when it goes; these are marks known to oneself, not visible to others.

line_issue: The line turns a portrait into a command and shrinks the three gunas' effects to 'moods'. Corrected: 'One who has gone beyond the three qualities does not hate clarity, activity or dullness when they arise, and does not long for them when they pass.'

claim: Alike in pain and pleasure, abiding in the self, regarding clod, stone and gold alike, steady, alike in blame and praise.

cultivates.why: pain and pleasure, praise and blame weigh the same
svastha: resting in one's own self
steady

needs: continues the portrait begun in 14.22

commentary.reading: Shankara: svastha means abiding in his own self, serene; the pleasant and unpleasant, blame and praise are alike to him.

claim: Alike in honour and dishonour, alike to friend and foe, having given up all undertakings, one is called beyond the gunas.

cultivates.why: honour and dishonour, friend and foe held alike
every self-driven undertaking is given up

needs: a seeker's ideal; not for someone disrespected or someone starting out

commentary.reading: Shankara: he gives up all undertakings for seen and unseen results, keeping only what maintains the body; these qualities, practised with effort by the seeker, become natural marks in the realised.

line_issue: 'Letting go of the need to start everything: free' misstates both halves. Corrected: 'The same in honour and dishonour, the same to friend and foe, having given up every self-driven undertaking: such a person is said to have gone beyond the three qualities.'

claim: Fearlessness, purity of heart, steadiness in knowledge and yoga, giving, self-control, sacrifice, study, austerity and uprightness mark the divine nature.

cultivates.why: fearlessness heads the list of the divine qualities
giving is named among them

commentary.reading: Shankara: these are the divine endowment; fearlessness is first, and purity of the inner organ is dealing without deceit. Krishna tells Arjuna in 16.5 that he is born to this nature.

claim: The demonic cling to measureless worry ending only at death, hold sense enjoyment as highest, convinced that this is all.

cultivates.why: ties endless worry to the belief that getting and enjoying is all there is

needs: only as a diagnosis of a materialist outlook; the speaker is describing the demonic nature, so it must never be shown to an anxious person as a mirror

commentary.reading: Shankara: those of demonic nature are given over to cares without measure that end only with death, and are sure that enjoyment of desires is the highest human goal.

claim: Bound by a hundred cords of hope, given to desire and anger, the demonic amass wealth unjustly for sense enjoyment.

heals.why: expectations are pictured as a hundred ropes pulling a person every way

cultivates.why: shows where unchecked wanting leads

needs: describes the demonic nature; never for someone under honest money stress

commentary.reading: Shankara: bound by hundreds of nooses of hope and dragged about by them, taking desire and anger as their refuge, they strive to gather wealth by unjust means.

claim: The demonic person thinks: this I gained today, this wish I will fulfil; this wealth is mine and more will be.

depicts.why: the inner voice of never enough, quoted word for word
each gain is already pointing at the next one

needs: serve as a mirror for the wanting mind, without the 'demonic' label attached to the reader

commentary.reading: Shankara: this is the thinking of those of demonic nature: this I have got now, this wish I shall attain, this wealth is mine and that too will be.

claim: Non-violence, truth, absence of anger, renunciation, peace, no slander, compassion to beings, non-covetousness, gentleness, modesty and steadiness mark the divine nature.

cultivates.why: compassion toward beings is named
peace and absence of anger are named

commentary.reading: Shankara: akrodha is calming the anger that arises when one is abused or struck; achapala is not moving speech, hands and feet without purpose.

claim: Vigour, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of malice and of excessive pride belong to one born to the divine nature.

cultivates.why: boldness and dignity are named first
forgiveness stands beside vigour, not in place of it
fortitude that lifts body and senses when they flag

commentary.reading: Shankara: tejas is boldness, not brightness of skin; kshama is the absence of inner agitation when abused or struck; dhriti is the function of mind that lifts up the tired body and senses.

claim: Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance belong to one born to the demonic nature.

cultivates.why: names the traits that take a person downward

needs: a reader examining pride or harshness; as a mirror it is a verdict

commentary.reading: Shankara: dambha is posing as righteous, darpa is the pride of wealth and kin, parushya is harsh speech; these are the demonic endowment, which leads to bondage (16.5).

claim: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint and purity of feeling are called austerity of mind.

heals.why: quiet and self-restraint are given as a daily discipline for the mind

cultivates.why: serenity of mind is named first
silence and restraint
gentleness and clean intent toward others

commentary.reading: Shankara: mauna here is restraint of mind that results in restraint of speech; bhava-samshuddhi is freedom from deceit in dealing with others.

claim: Austerity done with show to gain respect, honour and reverence is rajasic, unstable and impermanent.

heals.why: effort made for an audience is shown to be shaky by nature

cultivates.why: asks whom the effort is for

commentary.reading: Shankara: austerity practised for praise, honour and worship, with display, gives a fleeting and uncertain result and is rajasic.

claim: A gift given as duty, to a worthy person who cannot repay, at the right place and time, is sattvic.

heals.why: giving with no return in view loosens the hold of 'mine'

cultivates.why: giving because it is right to give

commentary.reading: Shankara: given with the thought 'it ought to be given', to one who has not helped and cannot repay, at a fit place and time and to a fit recipient.

claim: A gift given for a return, or with an eye to reward, or reluctantly, is rajasic.

heals.why: names the hidden expectation inside giving, which later turns to resentment

cultivates.why: a test of one's own motive in giving

commentary.reading: Shankara: given so that the other will help in return, or aiming at an unseen reward, or with reluctance; such a gift is rajasic.

line_issue: The verse classes such giving as rajasic; it does not say it is not giving. Corrected: 'A gift given to get something back, or for a reward, or grudgingly, is giving driven by restless desire.'

claim: An embodied being cannot give up action entirely; one who gives up the fruit of action is called a renouncer.

heals.why: the choice is not between working and quitting; what can be dropped is the claim on the payoff

cultivates.why: renunciation is relocated from the work to its fruit

commentary.reading: Shankara: one who identifies with the body cannot abandon action completely; so the one who gives up the fruit while doing obligatory work is called a renouncer, by way of praise.

claim: The seat, the doer, the various instruments, the distinct efforts, and providence as fifth are the five causes of action.

heals.why: the doer is one of five causes, so a result that failed was never yours alone
much of what decides an outcome was never in your hands

cultivates.why: sees an action as the work of many factors
credit and blame are both shared

commentary.reading: Shankara: the body as seat, the agent, the senses as instruments, the various functions of the vital airs, and the presiding deities as the fifth; 18.16 adds that one who sees himself as the sole doer does not see.

claim: The doer who is undisciplined, crude, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent and procrastinating is called tamasic.
needs: a reader who can take a hard mirror; it places despondency beside deceit and malice

commentary.reading: Shankara: vishadi is one always sunk in dejection, dirghasutri one who puts off for a month what should be done today; such a doer is tamasic.

claim: The intellect that knows action and withdrawal, duty and non-duty, fear and fearlessness, bondage and freedom, is sattvic.

heals.why: describes the clear judgement that can tell when to act and when to step back
clear understanding knows what is truly to be feared and what is not

cultivates.why: discernment of what should and should not be done

commentary.reading: Shankara: pravritti is the path of action and nivritti the path of renunciation; the intellect that knows these, with their causes of fear and fearlessness, bondage and release, is sattvic.

claim: Each person devoted to his own work attains perfection; Krishna will explain how.

heals.why: one's own ordinary work is named as a road to fulfilment

cultivates.why: delight in one's own work
no need to look to another's work

needs: read with 18.46, which says how

commentary.reading: Shankara: devoted to the work proper to him, a person gains the perfection of fitness for knowledge. Ramanuja likewise takes one's own work, done as worship, as the means.

claim: By worshipping through one's own work the One from whom all beings arise and who pervades all, a person attains perfection.

heals.why: work that felt pointless becomes an offering to the source of life

cultivates.why: one's own work as worship
work offered to the One who pervades all
gives ordinary work a reason

needs: a reader open to God

commentary.reading: Shankara: worshipping with his own duty the Lord from whom beings proceed and by whom all is pervaded, a person gains the perfection of fitness for knowledge. Ramanuja: one's work is itself the worship.

claim: One should not abandon work born of one's nature though faulty; all undertakings are clouded by fault as fire by smoke.

heals.why: flaws in the work are no reason to drop it; every undertaking has them
imperfection is the condition of all work, not proof of unfitness

cultivates.why: staying with one's work through its faults
keeps a resolve from breaking on the first flaw

commentary.reading: Shankara: one should not give up the work one is born to, though it has faults, since all undertakings, one's own or another's, are covered by fault as fire by smoke.

claim: Giving up ego, force, arrogance, desire, anger and possessions, free of mine and peaceful, one becomes fit to be Brahman.

heals.why: ego is the first thing set down
arrogance and force are given up

cultivates.why: peace when 'mine' is gone
giving up possessions and the sense of mine
fitness for becoming Brahman

needs: a seeker far along; the passage 18.51-53 describes the renunciate's final discipline

commentary.reading: Shankara: having given up even the possessions kept for the body's upkeep, as a renunciate without 'mine' and at peace, he becomes fit for being Brahman.

line_issue: 'You become peaceful' drops the verse's goal. Corrected: 'Having let go of ego, force, arrogance, desire, anger and grasping, with no sense of mine and at peace, a person becomes fit to be one with Brahman.'

claim: One who has become Brahman, serene, neither grieves nor craves; alike to all beings, he gains supreme devotion to Krishna.

cultivates.why: the serene self of one established in Brahman
the same toward all beings
the highest devotion arises from this state

needs: a seeker's horizon; to a griever 'does not grieve' reads as a verdict

commentary.reading: Shankara: having attained Brahman and a serene self, he does not grieve over any loss or long for anything; he gains the supreme devotion which is knowledge. Ramanuja reads supreme devotion as the direct fruit of seeing the self.

line_issue: The line drops both 'become Brahman' and the supreme devotion. Corrected: 'One who has become one with Brahman is serene, and neither grieves nor craves. The same toward all beings, such a person gains the highest devotion to me.'

claim: With mind fixed on Krishna one crosses all difficulties by his grace; refusing to listen out of ego, one perishes.

heals.why: every difficulty is crossed by grace when the mind rests in him
the crossing does not depend on one's own strength alone

cultivates.why: keeping the mind on him
trust in grace

needs: a devotional reader; the second half is a teacher's warning to Arjuna and is harsh without the scene

commentary.reading: Shankara: with mind on the Lord you will cross all the hard places of samsara by his grace; if from ego, thinking yourself learned, you do not heed, you will be ruined.

claim: Taking refuge in the Lord alone with one's whole being, one attains by his grace supreme peace and the eternal abode.

heals.why: the whole weight is placed on the Lord who dwells in the heart
refuge with one's whole being

cultivates.why: taking refuge with all one's being
supreme peace is promised through grace

needs: a devotional reader; 'him' is the Lord seated in the heart of all beings (18.61)

commentary.reading: Shankara: go for refuge with your whole being to the Lord who dwells in the hearts of all; by his grace you will gain the highest peace and the eternal state. Ramanuja reads it as the call to surrender to the inner ruler.

claim: By Krishna's grace Arjuna's delusion is destroyed and memory regained; firm and free of doubt, he will do Krishna's word.

depicts.why: 'I stand firm, I will do as you say', the resolve spoken by the man who had put down his bow
confusion gone, clarity returned

cultivates.why: shows what resolve sounds like after real doubt
he credits the clearing to grace

needs: the whole arc from 2.7; a closing verse for the last day of a plan, never early

commentary.reading: Shankara: the delusion born of ignorance is destroyed and the memory of the true nature of the self is regained by the Lord's grace; this is the fruit of the whole scripture.

line_issue: The line drops 'by your grace' and turns 'I will do as you say' into 'I'll act'. Corrected: 'My confusion is gone and my memory has returned, by your grace. I stand firm, free of doubt. I will do as you say.'

claim: Giving up work as painful, from fear of bodily strain, is rajasic renunciation and wins no fruit of renunciation.

heals.why: separates quitting because a thing is wrong from quitting because it is hard

cultivates.why: a test of one's motive for stopping
staying with a duty through discomfort

needs: a reader weighing whether to quit out of discomfort; not for someone exhausted or being harmed by their work

commentary.reading: Shankara: one who abandons obligatory work as painful, from fear of bodily trouble, makes a rajasic renunciation and does not gain liberation, the fruit of renunciation with knowledge.

claim: Never was there a time when Krishna, Arjuna or these kings did not exist, nor will any ever cease to be.

heals.why: the one you mourn has not stopped being
no one ceases to be

cultivates.why: the self is present in all three times

needs: openness to a self that outlasts the body; not the first word to a fresh loss

commentary.reading: Shankara: in all three periods of time we are eternal as the self; the plural refers to the bodies, not to many selves. Ramanuja reads the plural as showing that selves are truly many and eternal.

claim: The steady person whom these contacts do not afflict, alike in pain and pleasure, becomes fit for immortality.

cultivates.why: the steady person is not thrown by what passes
alike in pain and pleasure

needs: follows 2.14 on bearing what comes and goes

commentary.reading: Shankara: the one who sees the eternal self and is not shaken by pleasure and pain becomes fit for immortality, which is liberation.

claim: Weapons do not cut the self, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, wind does not dry it.

heals.why: nothing that can happen to the body reaches what you are
what was essential in the one who died could not be harmed

cultivates.why: the self is beyond the reach of the elements
nothing can cut, burn, drown or wither it

needs: openness to a self distinct from the body

commentary.reading: Shankara: being without parts, the self cannot be cut by weapons, burnt by fire, wetted by water or dried by wind.

claim: Beings are unmanifest in the beginning, manifest in the middle and unmanifest again at the end; what is there to lament?

heals.why: a life is the visible middle of something whose beginning and end are unseen

cultivates.why: sees a life as an appearing between two unseen states

needs: distance from the loss; the closing question dismisses lament and stings a fresh griever

commentary.reading: Shankara: bodies, the aggregates of cause and effect, are unseen before they arise and after they perish; what lament is fitting for what is seen only for a while, like an illusion?

claim: Arjuna must not yield to unmanliness, which does not befit him; he should cast off petty faint-heartedness and rise.

cultivates.why: inside the scene: a friend reminds a brave man who he is
'rise'

needs: the scene: a charioteer and friend speaking to a great warrior moments before battle; alone it calls a struggling reader's distress petty

commentary.reading: Krishna's first words are a rebuke meant to rouse Arjuna; the teaching proper begins only at 2.11, after Arjuna surrenders as a student in 2.7. Shankara does not comment on the verses before 2.11.
commentary.source: Plain sense; Sridhara and Madhusudana on 2.2-3 (from memory)

line_issue: The line softens a rebuke into reassurance and hides that it is one; shown alone it still tells a struggling person their distress is small. Keep it inside its scene. Corrected: 'Do not give way to this, Arjuna. It does not suit you. Put down this faintness of heart and stand up.'

claim: The resolute understanding is single; the thoughts of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.

depicts.why: the undecided mind is pictured splitting into endless branches

heals.why: shows that the branching comes from not having settled on one aim
one settled understanding gathers the mind

cultivates.why: a decided mind is single
one clear conviction instead of many

commentary.reading: Shankara: the understanding that is resolute, born of the right means of knowledge, is one; the notions of those without it are endless and many-branched, and spread samsara wide.

claim: Action for reward is far inferior to the yoga of understanding; seek refuge in understanding; pitiable are those moved by fruit.

heals.why: working only for the payoff is named as a poverty
shelter is offered in an even understanding, not in the outcome

cultivates.why: taking refuge in understanding
the even mind of 2.48 is the understanding meant

commentary.reading: Shankara: action done by one seeking results is far lower than action done with evenness of mind; kripana, the pitiable, are those who work for fruit, like the one who leaves the world without knowing the imperishable.

claim: When the intellect, confused by what it has heard, stands unmoving and steady in samadhi, one attains yoga.

depicts.why: a mind pulled this way and that by everything it has heard

heals.why: the wobbling ends when the understanding settles in stillness
confusion from conflicting voices is expected, and it can settle

cultivates.why: an understanding that stands unmoving

commentary.reading: Shankara: the intellect is distracted by hearing of many ends and means; when it stands without doubt, unmoving in samadhi, the self, then you gain the yoga of discriminating wisdom.

claim: One who gives up all desires of the mind and is content in the self alone is called steady in wisdom.

heals.why: contentment is found in the self, so wanting has nothing left to fetch

cultivates.why: content in the self by the self
the self is itself the source of satisfaction
desires that live in the mind are let go

commentary.reading: Shankara: having given up all desires, satisfied in the inmost self alone with no need of outer gain, like one who has tasted nectar; such a knower is called steady in wisdom.

claim: One without attachment anywhere, who neither rejoices at good nor hates bad when it comes, has firmly established wisdom.

heals.why: the bad that comes is met without hatred

cultivates.why: no elation at the good, no bitterness at the bad
without clinging anywhere

needs: not a reply to fresh grief or injury

commentary.reading: Shankara: without affection even for body and life, he neither praises on gaining the pleasant nor hates on meeting the unpleasant; his discriminating wisdom is established.

claim: Arjuna does not know which is better, to conquer or be conquered; those whose death would make life unwanted stand before him.

depicts.why: either outcome is a loss: he cannot say which is better
'we do not know', said plainly
the people he would not want to live without are on the other side

commentary.reading: Plain sense, as Sridhara and Gita Press give it: Arjuna cannot decide whether victory or defeat is better, since the kinsmen whose killing would make life unwanted stand facing him.

line_issue: 'Or even what winning would look like' is invented and the weight of the verse is dropped. Corrected: 'I cannot tell which would be better, to win or to lose. The very people I would not want to live without are standing against me.'

claim: The turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind even of a wise person who is striving.

heals.why: being pulled off course happens even to the wise who are trying; it is not a personal failing
the pull of the senses is named as strong, so a slip is no surprise

commentary.reading: Shankara: the senses are turbulent and carry off by force the mind even of a discerning person who keeps trying; hence they must be restrained (2.61).

line_issue: 'Don't be surprised; be ready' is an instruction the verse does not give. Corrected: 'Even a wise person who is trying hard can have the mind carried off by the restless senses.'

claim: The self-controlled one who moves among objects with senses free of attraction and aversion attains serenity.

heals.why: one can live among things without being pulled by them
aversion is dropped along with attraction

cultivates.why: serenity is the promised fruit
free of both grabbing and pushing away

commentary.reading: Shankara: the answer to the chain of 2.62-63: one who uses the unavoidable objects with senses free from attraction and aversion, mind under control, attains serenity.

claim: The mind that follows the roving senses carries away one's wisdom as wind carries a boat on water.

heals.why: shows the mechanism: the mind follows one sense and the whole understanding is blown off course

cultivates.why: seeing which sense the mind is trailing

commentary.reading: Shankara: the mind that runs after the senses as they move among their objects carries off the discriminating wisdom, as wind drives a boat off its course.

claim: One who gives up all desires and lives free of longing, without mine or ego, attains peace.

heals.why: peace is placed where longing ends
'I' and 'mine' are what is set down
nothing is claimed as mine

cultivates.why: peace is the stated fruit
moving through life without longing

commentary.reading: Shankara: the renunciate who gives up all desires and moves about with only the effort needed to keep the body, without 'mine' or 'I', attains the peace of nirvana.

claim: One should always do the work that must be done without attachment; acting unattached, a person attains the supreme.

heals.why: the work is done fully and the claim on it is dropped

cultivates.why: work without clinging
'always' do what has to be done

commentary.reading: Shankara: therefore do the obligatory work without attachment; doing it for the Lord's sake, a person reaches liberation through purity of mind.

claim: Krishna's seemingly mixed words confuse Arjuna's understanding; he asks for the one sure thing leading to the highest good.

depicts.why: the advice he has heard seems to point two ways
'you are confusing my understanding'
he asks for the one thing that is surely best

commentary.reading: Shankara: Arjuna takes the praise of knowledge and the command to act as contradictory; 'as if' shows the Lord's words are not truly mixed, only seem so to him.

claim: Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone; one should act also with a view to the welfare of the world.

heals.why: when personal goals no longer pull, there is still the good of the world to work for

cultivates.why: acting for the holding together of the world
kings like Janaka reached the highest while working

commentary.reading: Shankara: Janaka and others sought perfection along with action; and to keep people from going astray, one should act for the welfare of the world.

claim: Krishna has no duty in the three worlds and nothing unattained to attain, yet he continues in action.

heals.why: having nothing left to gain is not a reason to stop; even God keeps working

cultivates.why: action continued purely for others

commentary.reading: Shankara: the Lord has nothing to do or gain in the three worlds, yet he acts, since people follow his path and would be ruined if he did not.

claim: The wise should not unsettle the minds of the ignorant attached to action, but engage them by acting steadily themselves.

heals.why: impatience with those who are not yet where you are is replaced by working beside them

cultivates.why: care not to shake someone's footing before they have another
teaching by doing the work oneself

commentary.reading: Shankara: the knower should not disturb the conviction of the unwise who are attached to action; doing the same work himself with a steady mind, he should lead them to do it.

claim: All actions are done by the gunas of nature; one deluded by ego thinks 'I am the doer'.

heals.why: the sense of being the sole doer is named as a confusion
success was the work of many forces

cultivates.why: separating what nature does from the one who watches
you are not the doer you take yourself to be

commentary.reading: Shankara: actions are done by the gunas, the modifications of nature in the form of body and senses; one whose mind is deluded by ego, identifying with them, thinks 'I am the doer'.

claim: Surrendering all actions to Krishna with mind on the self, free of hope and mine, one should fight with fever gone.

heals.why: the inner fever about how it will go is what gets put down
acting without hoping for a particular return

cultivates.why: every action is handed to God
no 'mine' in the work

needs: a reader open to offering work to God

commentary.reading: Shankara: resign all actions to the Lord with the thought 'I act as a servant for the Lord', without expectation or ownership; 'fever' is anguish and grief.

line_issue: 'Something higher' blurs the speaker; the verse says 'to me'. Corrected: 'Hand all your work to me, keep your mind on the self, drop the hoping and the mine, and act with the fever gone.'

claim: Even the wise act according to their own nature; beings follow nature, so what can repression accomplish?

heals.why: the pull of one's nature is common to everyone, even the wise; force alone was never going to work

cultivates.why: working with one's nature instead of only clamping down on it

needs: read with 3.34, which says where effort does work; alone it can sound like 'nothing can change'

commentary.reading: Shankara: nature is the impressions of past deeds showing up in this life; everyone acts by it. He then raises the objection that effort is useless, and 3.34 answers: do not come under like and dislike.

claim: Attraction and aversion are lodged in each sense toward its objects; one should not come under their sway, for they are enemies.

heals.why: liking is named as a waylayer, not a guide
disliking is named the same way

cultivates.why: noticing like and dislike before they decide for you

commentary.reading: Shankara: this is the scope of human effort: nature moves a person only through like and dislike, so one who checks these with their opposite is no longer under nature's rule.

claim: Arjuna asks what impels a person to commit sin even unwillingly, as if driven by force.

depicts.why: 'why do I do the wrong thing even when I do not want to', asked without excuse
the sense of being pushed by something stronger than one's will

commentary.reading: Plain sense, as in Shankara: Arjuna asks for the cause that drives a person to wrong like a servant ordered by a king, though unwilling.

claim: As fire is covered by smoke, a mirror by dust and an embryo by the womb, so knowledge is covered by desire.

heals.why: clear sight is covered, not destroyed; the three images show covers that come off
desire is shown as what clouds judgement

cultivates.why: knowing that wanting distorts seeing

commentary.reading: Shankara: 'this' is knowledge, as 3.39 states; desire covers it. Later commentators such as Madhusudana read the three images as three depths of covering, light, middling and thick.

claim: Not by abstaining from action does one reach actionlessness, nor by mere renunciation does one attain perfection.

heals.why: not starting is not freedom
walking away does not by itself deliver what one hopes

cultivates.why: freedom from action is an inner state, not an absence of activity

commentary.reading: Shankara: actionlessness, the state of abiding in knowledge, is not reached by not undertaking actions; action purifies the mind and is the means to it.

claim: Knowing the self as higher than intellect and steadying the self by the self, one should slay the enemy that is desire.

heals.why: desire is fought from a place in you that stands above it

cultivates.why: there is that in you which is higher than mind and intellect
steadying oneself by oneself
holding firm against an enemy hard to overcome

needs: the ladder of 3.42: senses, mind, intellect, and that which is beyond

commentary.reading: Shankara: knowing the self as beyond the intellect and composing the mind by the purified mind, slay the enemy in the form of desire.

claim: No one can remain even a moment without acting; everyone is made to act helplessly by the gunas born of nature.

heals.why: doing nothing is not actually an available option

cultivates.why: since one will act anyway, the question is only how

commentary.reading: Shankara: this is said of the unknowing; all are driven to act by sattva, rajas and tamas. The knower, unmoved by the gunas, is a separate case.

claim: One who restrains the organs of action but dwells mentally on sense objects is deluded and called a hypocrite.

cultivates.why: holding back outwardly while feeding the craving inwardly is not restraint

commentary.reading: Shankara: one who holds back hands and feet but keeps thinking of objects is of deluded mind, a mithyachara, one of false conduct.

claim: Having given up attachment to fruit, ever content and dependent on nothing, he does nothing though fully engaged in action.

heals.why: ever content, so the work is not done to fill a lack
fully busy and yet inwardly not labouring

cultivates.why: always satisfied
no clinging to what the work brings
the knower acts and is not the doer

commentary.reading: Shankara: nirashraya is without dependence on any means to a desired end; because he sees the actionless self, he does nothing at all even while engaged in action.

line_issue: 'Leaning on no one's approval' narrows 'dependent on nothing', and 'he does nothing at all' is lost. Corrected: 'Having let go of the claim on results, always content and leaning on nothing, such a person is fully at work and yet does nothing at all.'

claim: The offering, the oblation, the fire and the offerer are Brahman; one absorbed in Brahman as action reaches Brahman.
